claim: Removing Brahui from the set of attested Dravidian languages and reporting the geographic measurement on the remaining languages shows something about where Dravidian was spoken - that the family's centre of gravity is southern and eastern and that Brahui's northwestern position is therefore anomalous and in need of a migration explanation.

notes: SUPERSEDED BY DMB-002. This row is the interpretation the owner challenged, written out in full so that it is not re-proposed. It is retained under the CLAUDE.md standing constraint that correction history is preserved and rejected reasoning stays visible. It is NOT deleted. Two distinct defects: (a) it reads a delete-one sensitivity statistic as a substantive claim about a language family's geography (BF-005); (b) it treats the twenty-odd attested Dravidian languages as independent points, which they are not if any of them subgroup (BF-006). Note the direction: the overstatement here favours a MIGRATION reading of Brahui, which is the reading the inherited record already REJECTED as the default (R-10, IH-156). claim: A leave-one-out distance statistic over attested Dravidian language locations measures how much of that statistic's value rests on a single language. Deleting Brahui and recomputing the distance from a northwestern reference to the nearest remaining language supports a statement about the instrument's exposure to one datapoint, and about the size of the gap between Brahui and the next-nearest attested Dravidian language. It does not support any statement about where Dravidian was spoken at any date: the statistic has no chronological term, the attested set is a survival sample rather than a sample of past distribution, and the reference point is a free parameter of the analyst's choosing.

claim: This measurement sits inside the scope of constitution section 4.M, Brahui, Kurukh and Malto, which requires six competing models to be held open: long-term northwestern survival; later long-distance migration; broader ancient distribution followed by language replacement; continuing dialect networks followed by fragmentation; small migrating group plus extensive local language adoption; and complex combinations. Treating Brahui as detachable from the Dravidian set - as a datapoint whose removal leaves the rest of the family intact and interpretable - presupposes the second or the fifth of those models, in which Brahui arrives from elsewhere and is therefore separable from a family whose real distribution lies elsewhere. Under the first, third and fourth models Brahui is not detachable, because on those models it is not an addition to the distribution but a survival of it.

claim: The Kurukh-Malto unit is strongly supported by the retrieved lexical data. Kurukh and Malto share 19 cognate sets exclusively - present in both and in no other variety - which is rank 1 of all 190 pairs, ahead of Koya-Telugu at 13 and Gondi-Koya at 7. Over the 95 concepts both attest they share a cognate set in 48.4% of cases, and each is the other's highest-sharing partner of the nineteen available.
locator: 04-AUDITS/north-dravidian-cognate-sharing.py sections 1 and 2; lexibank/dravlex cldf/cognates.csv at 3757807

Measurement and bibliography agree here. Still an upper bound on shared innovations, not a count of them: an exclusive set is equally consistent with a joint innovation and with a Proto-Dravidian retention lost in the other eighteen.

claim: Brahui's attachment to the Kurukh-Malto unit is NOT supported by the retrieved lexical data. Brahui shares 1 cognate set exclusively with Kurukh and 1 exclusively with Malto, against the 19 Kurukh and Malto share with each other. Brahui-Kurukh sharing over the 100 concepts both attest is 22.0%, which ranks seventh of Brahui's nineteen possible partners, below Parji at 34.4%, Ollari_Gadba at 25.4%, Kuwi at 25.0%, Tulu at 23.5%, Tamil at 23.0% and Kannada at 22.0%. Brahui-Malto is 17.9%, which ranks fifteenth of nineteen. Among all 190 pairs, Brahui-Kurukh ranks 162nd and Brahui-Malto 183rd.

notes: The direct answer to the measurement the owner asked for, and it does not come out the way objection 2's antecedent assumes. Three cautions, all of which cut toward caution and not toward a stronger negative. (1) Brahui is lexically distant from everything: its best partner reaches 34.4% where the median pair reaches 38.5%, so its low scores with Kurukh and Malto are partly a general effect. (2) Brahui's three top-ranked partners - Parji, Ollari_Gadba, Kuwi - are exactly the three lowest-coverage varieties in the dataset at 64, 59 and 56 concepts, so those ranks are the least reliable numbers in the table and should not be read as a Brahui-Central Dravidian finding. (3) See DMB-020 for what this instrument structurally cannot see.

claim: Brahui, Kurukh and Malto share 2 cognate sets exclusively: concept 42_horn (Brahui maɾgʰ, Kurukh maɾag, Malto maɾgadu) and concept 78_smoke (Brahui mo:ʃ, Kurukh mosaga, Malto mo:ha). That is rank 4 of all 1140 triples on the raw count and rank 6 of 1140 once normalised by the 95 concepts all three attest, at 2.11 exclusive sets per 100. The rank flatters the result: the median triple scores 0, the top triple scores only 3, and 4 triples tie at 2, so a high rank here is worth two lexical items and no more.

Both words are also of a shape that invites a contact explanation as readily as a descent one, and this instrument cannot adjudicate that. claim: This instrument cannot see the evidence that Krishnamurti's North Dravidian actually rests on. DravLex is a 100-concept lexical wordlist. The conventional case for North Dravidian is phonological and morphological, and no phonological or morphological comparative data for Brahui, Kurukh or Malto was retrievable in this session. The absence of support at DMB-018 and DMB-019 is therefore typed NOT PRODUCED - the instrument does not generate evidence of the required kind - and NOT ACCESSIBLE for the rest, per HOLD-002 and SRC-052. It is NOT ABSENT DESPITE ADEQUATE SEARCH, and it is not a refutation of the subgroup.

claim: The instrument is not independent of the hypothesis. DravLex's cognate coding lists Krishnamurti 2003 among its five underlying sources, and Glottolog's North Dravidian node cites Krishnamurti 2003 and nothing else - as do its Central and South Dravidian nodes. The standard classification and the comparative dataset are therefore not two sources agreeing; they are one book, re-encoded twice. Krishnamurti 2003 has never been read in this project and stands at 'Named, not read'.

claim: Brahui has the highest proportion of singleton cognate sets of any variety in the dataset: 63 of its 104 sets, 60.6%, are attested in Brahui and no other Dravidian variety. Malto follows at 47.7% and Kurukh at 39.4%; the lowest are Kodava at 3.9% and Parji at 4.7%.
locator: 04-AUDITS/north-dravidian-cognate-sharing.py section 4
notes: Recorded because it is the observation most likely to be misused, and it is symmetrically misusable. A 60.6% singleton rate is consistent with early divergence from the rest of Dravidian, which favours the relict and broader-ancient-distribution models; it is equally consistent with heavy lexical replacement under Balochi and Indo-Aryan contact, which is independently expected on any model and is what constitution 4.M means by keeping loanword history separate from language history. Seven of Brahui's hundred forms are loan-flagged in this dataset, which is a floor on borrowing and not an estimate of it, since the flag records identified loans only. This row establishes nothing about dating and must not be cited as if it did.

A proposal that relates Dravidian to Elamite bears directly on how a northwestern Dravidian language is positioned, since it supplies an alternative account of northwestern Dravidian-like material that does not require the Brahui population to have arrived from anywhere in India.
